reference.source: Standard gynaecology textbook and vulval pain society guidance
clinicalPearls: Vulvodynia is chronic vulval pain, usually burning, stinging, or rawness, present for at least several months with no identifiable clinical or laboratory cause, making it a diagnosis of exclusion
It is subclassified by site into localised (most often provoked vestibulodynia at the vestibule) and generalised forms, and by whether pain is provoked, spontaneous, or mixed
Provoked vestibulodynia typically causes entry dyspareunia and pain on tampon insertion or tight clothing, with tenderness reproduced by light touch of the vestibule
Generalised vulvodynia produces more diffuse, often spontaneous neuropathic pain that may be unprovoked and less clearly localised
Examination is frequently normal apart from focal tenderness, and the cotton-swab (Q-tip) test helps map painful points at the vestibule
Associated features often include pelvic floor muscle overactivity, anxiety, and other chronic pain conditions, reflecting a component of central sensitisation

Management is multimodal and generic, combining vulval care advice, pelvic floor physiotherapy, psychological and pain-focused therapies, topical or systemic neuromodulating treatment, and occasionally surgery for refractory localised disease
The diagnosis should only be made after infective, dermatological, neurological, and neoplastic causes of vulval pain have been excluded
reference.pathophysiology: Vulvodynia is understood as a chronic pain condition rather than a structural disease. In localised provoked vestibulodynia, increased density and sensitisation of nociceptive nerve fibres in the vestibular mucosa, together with local inflammatory and hormonal influences, lower the threshold for pain so that normally innocuous touch is felt as burning. Peripheral sensitisation is compounded by amplification within the spinal cord and brain (central sensitisation) and by reflex overactivity and guarding of the pelvic floor musculature. Generalised vulvodynia is thought to reflect a more neuropathic, spontaneous pain process. Psychological factors and comorbid pain syndromes modulate the experience but are not the primary cause.
additionalDifferentials: Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis or other infection
Lichen sclerosus, lichen planus, or contact dermatitis
additionalInvestigations: Cotton-swab (Q-tip) test to localise and grade vestibular tenderness
Vaginal swabs and microscopy to exclude infection
Vulval examination for dermatoses, with biopsy of any abnormal area
Assessment of pelvic floor tone and tenderness
Oestrogen status assessment in peri- or postmenopausal women
Screening for anxiety, depression, and comorbid chronic pain to guide holistic care
redFlags: Visible ulcer, mass, or persistent abnormal lesion requiring biopsy to exclude malignancy
Neurological deficit or dermatomal pain suggesting a specific neuropathy
Features of active infection or a dermatosis that would reclassify the pain as having an identifiable cause
Rapidly worsening pain or systemic symptoms
reference.prognosis: Vulvodynia is a chronic relapsing condition, but many women improve substantially with a combined, individualised approach; provoked vestibulodynia in particular can respond well to physiotherapy and neuromodulation, though complete and permanent resolution is not guaranteed.
pitfalls: Repeatedly treating presumed thrush without confirming infection and overlooking a pain syndrome
Labelling the pain as purely psychological and failing to address peripheral and pelvic floor contributions
Making the diagnosis without first excluding dermatoses, infection, and neoplasia
Neglecting pelvic floor assessment, which is frequently abnormal and treatable
Offering surgery before adequate conservative and medical management in localised disease
